{{Short description|Concept in complex dynamics}}
In mathematics, and particularly [[complex dynamics]], the '''escaping set''' of an [[entire function]] <math>f</math> consists of all points that tend to infinity under the [[iterated function|repeated application]] of <math>f</math>.<ref name="RS">
{{cite journal|first1=P. J.|last1=Rippon|first2=G|last2=Stallard|author2-link= Gwyneth Stallard|
title=On questions of Fatou and Eremenko|journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]|year=2005|volume=133|issue=4|pages=1119–1126|doi=10.1090/s0002-9939-04-07805-0|doi-access=free}}</ref>
That is, a [[complex number]] <math>z_0\in\mathbb{C}</math> belongs to the escaping set if and only if the sequence defined by <math>z_{n+1} := f(z_n)</math> converges to infinity as <math>n</math> gets large. The escaping set of <math>f</math> is denoted by <math>I(f)</math>.<ref name="RS" />

For example, for <math>f(z)=e^z</math>, the origin <math>z=0</math> belongs to the escaping set, since the sequence <math>0,1,e,e^e,e^{e^e},\dots</math> tends to infinity.

== History ==
The iteration of transcendental entire functions was first studied by [[Pierre Fatou]] in 1926<ref name="Fatou">
{{cite journal|first=P.|last=Fatou|author-link=Pierre Fatou|title=Sur l'itération des fonctions transcendantes Entières|journal=Acta Math.|year=1926|volume=47|issue=4|pages=337–370|doi=10.1007/bf02559517|doi-access=free}}</ref>
The escaping set occurs implicitly in his study of the explicit entire functions <math>f(z)=z+1+\exp(-z)</math> and <math>f(z)=c\sin(z)</math>.

{{unsolved|mathematics|Can the escaping set of a transcendental entire function have a bounded component?}}
The first study of the escaping set for a general transcendental entire function is due to [[Alexandre Eremenko]] who used [[Wiman-Valiron theory]].<ref name="E">
{{cite journal
|last=Eremenko
|author-link=Alexandre Eremenko
|first=A|title=On the iteration of entire functions|year=1989|
journal=Banach Center Publications, Warsawa, PWN|volume=23|pages=339–345|doi=10.4064/-23-1-339-345
|url=http://www.math.purdue.edu/~eremenko/dvi/banach.pdf}}</ref>
He conjectured that every [[connected component (topology)|connected component]] of the escaping set of a transcendental entire function is unbounded. This has become known
as ''Eremenko's conjecture''.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="RRRS">{{cite journal|first1=G|last1=Rottenfußer|
first2=J|last2=Rückert|first3=L|last3=Rempe|author3-link=Lasse Rempe|first4=D|last4=Schleicher|
title=Dynamic rays of bounded-type entire functions|journal=Ann. of Math.|volume=173|year=2011|pages=77–125|
arxiv=0704.3213|doi=10.4007/annals.2010.173.1.3}}</ref> In 2021, a paper by Martí-Pete, [[Lasse Rempe|Rempe]], and Waterman constructed a counterexample to Eremenko's conjecture.<ref>
{{cite arXiv|first1=David|last1=Martí-Pete|first2=Lasse|last2=Rempe|first3=James|last3=Waterman|title=Eremenko's conjecture, wandering Lakes of Wada, and maverick points|date=2024-10-30|class=math.DS|eprint=2108.10256}}
</ref>

Eremenko also asked whether every escaping point can be connected to infinity by a curve in the escaping set; it was later shown that this is not the case. Indeed,
there exist entire functions whose escaping sets do not contain any curves at all.<ref name="RRRS" />

== Properties ==
The following properties are known to hold for the escaping set of any non-constant and non-linear entire function. (Here ''nonlinear'' means that the function is not of the form <math>f(z)=az+b</math>.)

* The escaping set contains at least one point.{{efn|Theorem 1 of (Eremenko, 1989)<ref name="E" />}}
* The [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] of the escaping set is exactly the [[Julia set]].{{efn|See (Eremenko, 1989),<ref name="E" /> formula (1) on p. 339 and l.2 of p. 340}} In particular, the escaping set is never [[closed set|closed]].
* For a transcendental entire function, the escaping set always intersects the Julia set.{{efn|Theorem 2 of (Eremenko, 1989)<ref name="E" />}} In particular, the escaping set is [[open set|open]] if and only if <math>f</math> is a polynomial.
* Every connected component of the closure of the escaping set is unbounded.{{efn|Theorem 3 of (Eremenko, 1989)<ref name="E" />}}
* The escaping set always has at least one unbounded connected component.<ref name="RS" />
* The escaping set is connected or has infinitely many components.<ref name="RS2" />
* The set <math>I(f)\cup \{\infty\}</math> is connected.<ref name="RS2">
{{cite journal|first1=P. J.|last1=Rippon|first2=G|last2=Stallard|
title=Boundaries of escaping Fatou components|journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]|year=2011|volume=139|issue=8|pages=2807–2820|doi=10.1090/s0002-9939-2011-10842-6|arxiv=1009.4450}}</ref>

Note that the final statement does not imply Eremenko's Conjecture. (Indeed, there exist connected spaces in which the removal of a single [[dispersion point]] leaves the remaining space totally disconnected.)

== Examples ==

=== Polynomials ===

A [[polynomial]] of degree 2 extends to an analytic self-map of the [[Riemann sphere]], having a [[Fixed point (mathematics)|super-attracting fixed point]] at infinity. The escaping set is precisely the [[attractor|basin of attraction]] of this fixed point, and hence usually referred to as the **basin of infinity**. In this case, <math>I(f)</math> is an [[open set|open]] and [[connected space|connected]] subset of the complex plane, and the [[Julia set]] is the boundary of this basin.

For instance the escaping set of the [[complex quadratic polynomial]] <math>f(z) = z^2</math> consists precisely of the complement of the closed [[Unit disk|unit disc]]:

:<math>I(f) = \{z\in\mathbb{C} \colon |z|  > 1 \}. </math>

===Transcendental entire functions===
[[File:Exp-esc.png|thumb|Escaping set of <math>(\exp(z)-1)/2</math>.]]

For [[Transcendental function|transcendental entire functions]], the escaping set is much more complicated than for polynomials: in the simplest cases like the one illustrated in the picture it consists of uncountably many curves, called ''hairs'' or ''rays''. In other examples the structure of the escaping set can be very different (a ''spider's web'').<ref>{{cite journal|first=D.J.|last=Sixsmith|title= Entire functions for which the escaping set is a spider's web|journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]|volume=151|issue=3|pages=551–571|year=2012|arxiv=1012.1303|doi=10.1017/S0305004111000582|bibcode=2011MPCPS.151..551S}}</ref> As mentioned above, there are examples of transcendental entire functions whose escaping set contains no curves.<ref name="RRRS" />

By definition, the escaping set is an [[Borel hierarchy|<math>F_{\sigma\delta}\text{ set}</math>]]. It is neither [[Gδ set|<math>G_{\delta}</math>]] nor [[Fσ set|<math>F_{\sigma}</math>]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Rempe |first=Lasse |author-link=Lasse Rempe-Gillen |arxiv=2006.16946 |title=Escaping sets are not sigma-compact |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=2020 |volume=150 |pages=171–177 |doi=10.1090/proc/15576 }}</ref> For functions in the exponential class <math>\exp(z)+a</math>, the escaping set is not <math>G_{\delta\sigma}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |first=D.S. |last=Lipham | arxiv=2010.13876 |title= Exponential Iteration and Borel Sets|journal=Computational Methods and Function Theory |date=2024|volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=473–484 |doi=10.1007/s40315-024-00526-7 }}</ref>

A comprehensive survey of escaping sets of transcendental functions is given in the paper of Bergweiler and Rempe.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=W.|last1=Bergweiler|first2=L.|last2=Rempe|arxiv=2507.11370|title=The escaping set in transcendental dynamics|journal=Jahrbuch über die Fortschritte der Mathematik|date=2025}}</ref>
